slides.title: Stereotypy redirects the daily behavioral repertoire
body: **Stereotypy** is repetitive, relatively invariant behavior without an apparent immediate goal, such as swaying or repeated pacing. Greco and colleagues measured these patterns in zoo-housed African and Asian elephants alongside feeding, locomotion, social contact and self-maintenance.

Observers recorded behavior during unmanaged periods, separating the elephants’ spontaneous activity from actions requested by caretakers. Daytime and nighttime observations also separated responses to different daily opportunities, rather than treating a short daytime visit as a complete behavioral record.

Stereotypic movement occupies time that could otherwise support a varied behavioral repertoire. Its interpretation depends on when it occurs, the individual’s history and available opportunities. Comparing active-time budgets places repetitive behavior alongside feeding and social activity, linking welfare assessment to the animal’s actual daily experience.

slides.title: Individuals differ sharply in repetitive movement
body: The elephant survey measured **active-time stereotypy**, the proportion of time spent performing repetitive behavior after inactive observations were excluded. The published daytime average was 15.5% of active time; among performers, individual values spanned 0.5–68.1%.

The nighttime average was 24.8%; performers ranged from 1.4–74.2%. The broad distributions mean that a herd average can conceal an individual spending much of its active period in repetitive movement. An elephant’s own record is therefore central to monitoring change.

Daytime and nighttime conditions differed in staff presence, feeding and access arrangements. The study’s individual-level measures connected these lived conditions to behavioral rates. An assessment based on repeated observations can identify whether a management change alters an individual’s repertoire rather than merely changing a group mean.

slides.title: Social separation predicts higher stereotypy
body: **Social separation** was quantified as the proportion of an elephant’s time housed without other elephants. Greco and colleagues found that more separately housed time predicted higher daytime stereotypic behavior rates after accounting for other retained social and life-history variables.

Measuring each elephant’s exposure distinguished its experience from a zoo’s total herd size. A facility can contain several elephants while particular individuals spend substantial periods alone. The relevant biological opportunity is access to compatible partners during the animal’s own day.

The authors hypothesized that restricted social opportunities contribute to repetitive behavior through frustration or altered social experience. The association supports examining separation schedules together with behavior records. Compatible contact supplies opportunities for investigation, touch and interaction that the simple presence of other elephants elsewhere cannot provide.

slides.title: Juvenile contact expands social opportunities
body: Time spent with juvenile elephants predicted lower daytime stereotypic behavior rates in the North American zoo survey. **Juveniles** are young animals beyond the earliest infant stage whose play, exploration and interactions contribute to the social activity of a herd.

The analysis considered juvenile contact together with separate housing, managed activities and transfer history. This distinguished one kind of social exposure from simply placing an animal in any group. Adult social experience can change when a developing calf introduces new patterns of interaction.

The authors proposed play and participation in calf-related activities as potential contributions to the association. Habitat observations in a separate Asian elephant study documented changing proximity and interactions as a calf and juvenile male matured. Social opportunities have biological content determined by partner identity and developmental stage.

slides.title: Transfer history accompanies persistent stereotypy
body: An **inter-zoo transfer** changes an elephant’s location and can also change its social partners, caretakers, feeding arrangements and daily routines. Greco and colleagues counted lifetime transfers and found that more transfers predicted higher stereotypic behavior rates.

Transfer history appeared in both the daytime and nighttime models. It connected an earlier life-history variable with behavior recorded during current housing, while social exposure and management variables described present conditions. The study therefore linked pathology to experience extending beyond one observation period.

The authors hypothesized that separation from familiar partners and adjustment to unfamiliar conditions contribute to the association. Monitoring before and after a move can distinguish an immediate response from a persistent change. Maintaining compatible relationships addresses the social component of a transfer as well as the transport event itself.

slides.title: Choice changes access to usable environments
body: **Indoor/outdoor choice** means that an elephant can move between available areas rather than having its location determined entirely by a closed gate. More time with this choice predicted lower nighttime stereotypic behavior rates in the zoo survey.

The measure described access experienced by an individual, not simply the total area of an exhibit. Open access can allow movement between thermal conditions, resting surfaces and social settings. The association connects a management arrangement with opportunities for self-directed behavior.

Brown and colleagues also associated greater indoor/outdoor choice with lower glucocorticoid measures in species-specific zoo analyses. Behavioral flexibility and endocrine activity provide complementary outcomes for evaluating access. Useful choice depends on both alternatives being available and suitable for the animal at the time it uses them.

slides.title: Social conflict increases self-directed actions
body: **Self-directed behavior** includes actions directed toward the elephant’s own body, such as mouth touching, head shaking, dust bathing and curling the trunk inward. Vilela and colleagues compared these actions in captive Asian elephants after aggression and during baseline observations.

The post-conflict context was associated with an estimated 39.8% increase in expected event counts. Comparing a victim’s behavior across contexts linked the response to a recent social event rather than interpreting every self-touch as a sign of distress.

Mouth touching, head shaking, dust bathing and inward trunk curling contributed prominently to the difference. These actions offer a rapid behavioral record after conflict, complementing slower endocrine measures. An observer can connect the initiating interaction with the subsequent pattern of bodily activity over a defined interval.

slides.title: Event counts and durations describe different responses
body: Vilela and colleagues separated **event behaviors**, counted as discrete occurrences, from **state behaviors**, recorded by the proportion of time occupied. A brief head shake and a prolonged trunk position therefore contributed different kinds of information.

Post-conflict increases were clearer for counted events than for the overall time spent in state behaviors. The distinction prevented a long-lasting posture from being treated as interchangeable with several short actions and clarified which components responded most strongly to aggression.

Matching the measurement to the action is central to behavioral physiology. Counts capture the repeated initiation of an action; durations capture sustained occupation of a state. Together, they describe how an acute social challenge redistributes behavior rather than reducing the entire response to a single undifferentiated stress score.

slides.title: Orientation toward an aggressor changes the response
body: After conflict, Asian elephants sometimes held the trunk oriented toward the aggressor. Vilela and colleagues quantified the time spent in this orientation and compared it with the rate of self-directed actions during the same post-conflict observations.

Higher self-directed behavior rates accompanied less time with the trunk directed toward the aggressor. This relationship connects two competing components of the response: bodily actions and sustained orientation toward a socially relevant individual.

The authors proposed that attention to the aggressor may suppress or compete with self-directed actions. That is a hypothesis about behavioral organization. Recording both responses preserves the biological sequence of conflict, orientation and subsequent action, providing a richer description than classifying the elephant as either stressed or unstressed.

slides.title: Social history changes baseline behavior
body: Changes in group composition created different social conditions during the Asian elephant study. The researchers compared each individual’s baseline self-directed actions and stereotypy across these conditions while also recording aggression received from other elephants.

Two individuals increased baseline self-directed behavior when their victimization rates were highest, although the strength of the pattern differed between individuals. An elephant never observed receiving aggression maintained especially low self-directed behavior rates throughout the study.

Baseline behavior can therefore shift with the social environment against which a post-conflict response is judged. Self-directed actions and stereotypy also had different individual patterns. Repeated monitoring preserves this distinction between relatively immediate changes around conflict and persistent repetitive movement associated with a longer behavioral history.

slides.title: Mouse CRH neurons coordinate stress responses
body: The **paraventricular nucleus**, or PVN, is a hypothalamic population involved in endocrine stress responses. Füzesi and colleagues targeted mouse neurons producing **corticotropin-releasing hormone**, or CRH, a peptide that initiates pituitary signaling within the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis.

The pituitary releases adrenocorticotropic hormone, which stimulates adrenal glucocorticoid secretion. The study identified CRH cells with a genetic reporter and expressed light-sensitive proteins selectively within this population, permitting neuronal activity to be manipulated while behavior was recorded.

These mouse experiments separate a defined neuronal population from a general description of stress. The same identified cells contribute to behavioral organization as well as hormonal output. Elephant studies measure downstream hormones and actions; the causal neuronal evidence presented here comes specifically from mice.

slides.title: Neuronal inhibition redistributes post-stress behavior
body: Füzesi and colleagues expressed **archaerhodopsin**, a light-driven proton pump, in mouse PVN CRH neurons. Illumination moved positive charge out of the cell, hyperpolarizing its membrane and reducing action-potential firing. Brain-slice recordings verified the physiological effect before behavioral testing.

After footshock, the researchers inhibited these cells during 15 min of observation. Grooming fell from about 181 s in fluorescent-protein controls to 79 s in the inhibition group. Rearing and walking occupied a greater fraction of the remaining behavior.

Selective inhibition changed the allocation of actions after the same stress exposure. The control animals received the light protocol without the inhibitory pump, separating illumination from the targeted physiological manipulation. CRH-neuron activity thus contributes to organizing the post-stress repertoire rather than simply increasing every form of movement.

slides.title: Channel activation recruits hormonal and motor outputs
body: **Channelrhodopsin-2** is a light-gated cation channel: blue illumination opens an inward-current pathway that depolarizes neurons. Füzesi and colleagues expressed it in mouse PVN CRH cells and verified that optical stimulation controlled their activity in brain slices.

Activation increased circulating **corticosterone**, the glucocorticoid measured in these mice, 15 min after stimulation began. The mean increase was about 5.33 µg/dL in channel-expressing mice compared with 0.53 µg/dL in fluorescent-protein controls receiving the same illumination.

The activated cells also promoted grooming in a familiar observation chamber without preceding footshock. In a separate footshock experiment, reducing corticosterone synthesis with metyrapone left stress-induced grooming present. Hormonal secretion and rapid behavioral control can therefore emerge as distinct outputs of the same stress-related neuronal population.

slides.title: PVN projections excite lateral hypothalamic neurons
body: The **lateral hypothalamus**, or LH, receives axons from the mouse PVN CRH population. Füzesi and colleagues recorded LH neurons while stimulating these axons, connecting an identified anatomical projection with a measurable synaptic response.

Light pulses elicited inward currents with an average onset latency of about 4.7 ms. Tetrodotoxin, which blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and action potentials, abolished the response. Adding 4-aminopyridine, a potassium-channel blocker that enhances terminal excitation, partially restored it during longer light pulses.

The pharmacological sequence supported a direct excitatory connection from the labeled axons. Responses survived picrotoxin, a GABA receptor antagonist, but were strongly reduced by DNQX, an AMPA/kainate glutamate-receptor antagonist. Glutamatergic synaptic transmission supplies a rapid route from stress-related PVN activity to hypothalamic behavioral control.

slides.title: Environmental context gates stress-related actions
body: The same CRH-neuron activation produced different amounts of mouse grooming in different environments. Füzesi and colleagues used identical 10-Hz stimulation for 5 min in a familiar chamber, a novel environment and the chamber associated with footshock.

Grooming increased during activation in both unfamiliar settings, but the response was smaller in the footshock chamber. In the novel environment, channel-expressing mice groomed for about 85 s compared with 9 s in controls; in the footshock chamber the corresponding values were about 40 and 6 s.

Neuronal activity interacts with the behavioral opportunities and threat cues supplied by the environment. Stress-related action is consequently context dependent even when stimulation is held constant. This experimentally controlled comparison explains why the location and recent social circumstances of an elephant matter when interpreting a repeated action.

Individual concentrations varied substantially, and the before–after comparisons did not reveal an overall increase for each male. Behavioral adjustments during introductions can therefore coexist with relatively stable delayed hormone measurements. slides.title: Festival conditions alter adrenal measurements
body: Kumar and colleagues collected dung from Asian elephants in Indian facilities, including animals participating in the Dussehra festival. Rehearsal and the final procession provided distinct working contexts that could be linked with noninvasive glucocorticoid measurements.

The same study examined body condition, age, sex and origin because these characteristics influenced the measurement within facilities. A context-specific record can distinguish the demands of a particular event from an animal’s ordinary range. Repeated measures around predictable activities support adjustments to workload and recovery opportunities.

slides.title: Seasonality shifts the endocrine reference range
body: In semi-captive Asian elephants in Myanmar, Ukonaho and colleagues measured fecal cortisol metabolites across cold, hot and monsoon seasons. **Seasonality** changes food availability, weather and energetic demands, supplying a physiological context for interpreting adrenal activity.

Predicted concentrations were approximately 101 ng/g in the cold season, 86 ng/g in the hot season and 81 ng/g during monsoon. The cold-to-monsoon decline was about 20%, despite the expectation that the hottest conditions might produce the greatest endocrine response.

Repeated sampling allowed seasonal patterns to be separated from individual identity and sampling location. The elephants were not performing work tasks during sampling. A reference range tied to season preserves naturally occurring variation, so an assessment compares a management-related change with the environmental conditions present at the time.

slides.title: Immune-cell ratios complement hormone measurements
body: A **heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio** compares two classes of circulating white blood cells and supplies another measure associated with physiological stress. Ukonaho and colleagues counted these cells in blood smears alongside hormone, body-weight and oxidative-balance measurements.

The oxidative markers also lacked the same seasonal response, and body weight declined in the hot season. Several measurements therefore describe different components of the elephant’s adjustment. slides.title: Habitat complexity creates functional opportunities
body: **Environmental complexity** includes the distribution and variety of resources an elephant can use, not just enclosure area. Glaeser and colleagues followed Asian elephants across an older habitat, construction and a new habitat with more distributed feeding, pools and manipulable features.

The new setting expanded opportunities to choose indoor or outdoor areas and to seek food at different locations. Most months allowed more than 20 h of outdoor access per day, while individuals actually chose roughly 6–20 h outside according to their own activity and conditions.

Available space and used space are different biological quantities. Distributed resources link movement to a goal, such as locating browse or reaching an overhead feeder. The resulting choices provide a mechanism by which habitat design changes sensory investigation, locomotion, foraging and social contact during the elephant’s day.

slides.title: GPS tracks reveal goal-directed habitat use
body: Glaeser and colleagues fitted elephants with GPS bracelets to record outdoor movement. **GPS tracking** estimates successive locations, allowing routes and distances to be compared with the placement of food, pools, dirt mounds and other habitat resources.

The recorded elephants used the full outdoor habitat rather than consistently remaining within one small preferred area. Tracks across seasons documented access to different resources under contrasting weather conditions, connecting enclosure design with the places actually visited by each elephant.

The movement record was combined with direct observations of behavior. Distributed and varied food sources encouraged searching across the habitat, while larger pools added water-related activity. Measuring routes together with their behavioral context distinguishes functional exploration from simply assuming that every additional meter represents a favorable change.

slides.title: More usable habitat changes walking individually
body: After habitat expansion, one adult female’s mean daily outdoor walking distance increased from 7.6 to 15.4 km. A second female already walked longer distances and changed from 17.3 to 17.6 km per day. Glaeser and colleagues therefore documented markedly different individual responses.

Removing estimated locomotor stereotypy from the distance record retained the first female’s increase, from 7.3 to 14.7 km. That comparison separated added functional movement from repeated pacing that could inflate a distance total without expanding the behavioral repertoire.

An intervention can change the opportunities most relevant to one individual while producing a smaller distance change in another. Resource access, prior movement and the form of locomotion determine the interpretation. Tracking each elephant before and after habitat change preserves these differences instead of judging success solely by a herd-wide walking target.

slides.title: Construction and adaptation alter adrenal patterns
body: The habitat study collected repeated fecal glucocorticoid measurements before, during and after construction. Each phase combined physical changes with different routines and opportunities, allowing physiological patterns to be compared within the same Asian elephants.

Several individuals had their highest concentrations and greatest variability during construction, followed by lower values in the new habitat. One adult female retained relatively elevated concentrations after the move, although her values declined immediately after introductions to new habitat areas.

Individual time courses reveal adaptation that a single pre–post sample would miss. Construction, introduction and established use of a habitat are distinct exposures. Linking endocrine records with behavior and resource use captures the transition from a changing environment to an environment the elephant can actively explore and use.

slides.title: Resource changes redistribute the activity budget
body: An **activity budget** records how an animal allocates time among defined actions. Glaeser and colleagues compared feeding, locomotion, exploration, social behavior and repetitive activity across the previous and new Asian elephant habitats.

The new habitat increased food-seeking opportunities through diverse feeding locations and devices. Repetitive behavior persisted at low rates in two females, with a decrease in frequency in one and a changed bout pattern in the other. The authors connected these patterns with independent foraging opportunities.

A changed budget describes the replacement of one pattern with other available actions. Seeking food recruits movement, trunk investigation and manipulation, whereas a predictable delivery point can concentrate anticipation near one location. Resource design therefore links the sensory and motor components of feeding with the time structure of daily behavior.

slides.title: Social access permits proximity and separation choices
body: **Social proximity** records whether an elephant is near another individual, whereas interaction records what the animals do together. The expanded-habitat study measured both, preserving the distinction between occupying nearby space and engaging in social behavior.

Overall proximity declined in the new habitat while social interactions were sustained or increased. The calf and juvenile male also changed their nearest-neighbor patterns as they matured, linking the spatial record with development and partner identity.

Usable social space permits approaching a partner for interaction and moving away for another activity. Close spacing at all times is therefore different from access to compatible company. Combining proximity with the kind of interaction and developmental history explains how a complex habitat can support both affiliation and independent behavior.

slides.title: Affiliation and dominance organize a shared habitat
body: **Affiliative behavior** consists of nonaggressive social actions, while **agonistic behavior** includes interactions that establish or challenge dominance. Glaeser and colleagues classified the functions of observed interactions rather than counting every encounter as the same social event.

slides.title: Distributed feeding engages movement and manipulation
body: Interactions with food-delivery resources comprised 31.5% of recorded resource interactions in the previous habitat and 83.0% in the new habitat. Overhead and timed feeders required Asian elephants to locate food and manipulate resources instead of relying on one delivery point.

Elephants pushed or moved logs and stumps beneath overhead feeders and stood on them to increase reach. Food access thus linked sensory investigation with problem solving and whole-body movement, using the trunk and other motor actions within a practical foraging sequence.

Shared resource interactions increased from 10.5% to 22.9%. Feeding opportunities consequently changed both individual activity and the social setting of resource use. The intervention’s functional content was the behavior made possible by the resources, including searching, reaching, moving objects and feeding near compatible partners.

slides.title: Continuous cameras extend the behavioral record
body: Fazio and colleagues used closed-circuit cameras, camera traps and direct observation software to monitor zoo-housed Asian elephants. Cameras covered indoor and outdoor areas, extending observation into periods when staff and visitors were absent.

Monitoring connected each action with location, time and social partners. This made nighttime rest, indoor stereotypy and preferred resting areas observable alongside daytime feeding. A care decision based on the resulting record can address conditions present during the full daily cycle rather than relying only on behavior visible during staffed hours.

slides.title: Daily schedules shape stereotypy and rest
body: Hourly camera records separated daytime activity from nighttime rest in the Asian elephant herd. Feeding occurred mainly between 07:00 and 20:00, while the operational sleep category was concentrated between 20:00 and 06:00.

Stereotypic behavior was least common during much of the period from 15:00 to 05:00, encompassing afternoon feeding and sleep. A midday increase coincided with staff lunch breaks and anticipation of later care activities, connecting repetitive movement with the daily timing of expected events.

Behavioral pathology has a temporal setting. Changing food availability or predictable routines can affect particular hours even if a daily average changes little. An hourly record preserves the relation among feeding, staff presence, rest and repetitive movement so that interventions can target the conditions surrounding the action.

Preserving access to these locations supports the animal’s own spatial choices, while monitoring changes can identify when a previously used resting site becomes less usable.

slides.title: Species differ in recumbent rest duration
body: Holdgate and colleagues used leg-mounted accelerometers to measure recumbence in zoo elephants. **Accelerometry** records changes in movement and orientation, allowing lying posture to be identified over periods that include nighttime.

African elephants averaged 2.1 h of recumbence per day, whereas Asian elephants averaged 3.2 h. Both species averaged about 3.1 nighttime bouts, but African bouts lasted roughly 39 min compared with 66 min in Asian elephants.

The species difference arose substantially through bout duration rather than a greater number of bouts. Recording both frequency and duration preserves that organization of rest. Individual daily records further reveal whether an elephant rests in short episodes, long episodes or very little recumbence under the current housing conditions.

slides.title: Rest patterns vary within the same individual
body: Repeated accelerometer measurements recorded the sequence of standing and lying over several days. Holdgate and colleagues found elephants that lay down little throughout the recording period and others that omitted recumbence on only one or two days.

Seven animals were classified as highly non-recumbent because total lying time was less than 1 h across five days. Other individuals showed intermittent non-recumbence. These patterns describe different temporal organizations that would be obscured by a single average daily duration.

Day-by-day records can relate a changed rest pattern to flooring, outdoor access, social arrangements or health. A repeated absence of lying and a single non-recumbent night prompt different questions about the animal’s opportunity to rest. Continuous observation therefore preserves the behavioral history needed to identify a meaningful change.

slides.title: Resting surfaces influence recumbent opportunity
body: Recumbence in the zoo study rose after 20:00 and peaked near 04:00, linking lying behavior with nighttime housing. Holdgate and colleagues then examined how experienced substrates and outdoor access were associated with the amount of rest.

African elephants spending any time on entirely hard concrete or stone aggregate substrates were recumbent about 0.6 h less per day. Asian elephants spending time on entirely soft grass, sand or rubber substrates were recumbent about 1.1 h more per day.

The surface supporting the body is therefore a functional part of the resting environment. Assessing nighttime access alongside the hourly profile identifies whether suitable surfaces are available when the animal normally lies down. Species-specific associations also support monitoring the elephant’s actual response rather than imposing one identical rest target on every individual.

slides.title: Male introductions can support predominantly affiliation
body: López Pérez and colleagues introduced Asian male elephants through limited tactile contact before full physical interaction. **Limited contact** allowed interaction across a barrier, providing a staged transition before animals shared unrestricted space.

Affiliative behavior predominated during both phases. Aggression was initially absent in the limited-contact phase and remained relatively infrequent; during full introductions it declined over time. Submissive behavior also remained uncommon across the recorded periods.

The sequence documents social opportunities beyond permanent separate housing of males. Staging the introductions allowed caretakers to observe how relationships developed before increasing physical access. Behavioral records of affiliation, aggression and submission supplied information about the actual social consequences of each phase rather than assuming compatibility from sex alone.

slides.title: Individuals follow different socialization trajectories
body: Although affiliation predominated in the male group, individual trajectories differed. López Pérez and colleagues recorded which male initiated each action and how rates changed across days of limited and full-contact introductions.

Several males reduced affiliation as the introductions progressed, while others increased it during full physical contact. Two males never initiated aggression during the study. The group pattern therefore contained distinct responses that mattered for evaluating particular relationships.

Repeated individual observation can guide the timing and partners of social access. A decreasing interaction rate may accompany an established relationship rather than worsening welfare, while repeated unwanted aggression has a different meaning. The function, recipient and timing of an action preserve the social biology underlying the numerical rate.

slides.title: Androgen measurements add reproductive context
body: **Androgens** are steroid hormones involved in male reproductive physiology. López Pérez and colleagues measured fecal androgen metabolites alongside glucocorticoid metabolites to examine social introductions within the males’ endocrine context.

Most males retained comparable androgen concentrations before and 48 h after introductions, while one showed a decrease. Concentrations varied substantially among individuals, and age also influenced the pattern of androgen change during full-contact introductions.

Reproductive physiology and social behavior must be interpreted together. A male’s affiliation, aggression and hormone record supply different information about the interaction period. Tracking them jointly retains individual reproductive context while allowing care decisions to respond to directly observed behavior and the development of compatible social relationships.

slides.title: Age mates accompany lower glucocorticoid levels
body: Parker and colleagues monitored wild young African elephants, including orphans and nonorphans, using repeated dung samples and known family composition. **Social support** was examined through available age mates and adult female caregivers rather than inferred from group membership alone.

More age mates accompanied lower average glucocorticoid metabolite concentrations. Orphan status itself showed no simple relationship with the measured concentrations, while individuals joining non-natal groups had lower average values than those remaining with their natal family.

The social context surrounding loss is biologically informative. Peer access can coexist with opportunities for affiliation and shared activity, and family history changes what a group represents for an individual. These field observations support considering partner composition when managing young elephants whose normal developmental relationships have been interrupted.

slides.title: Resource conditions shape wild endocrine variation
body: The wild orphan study measured vegetation with a **normalized difference vegetation index**, a satellite-based measure of landscape greenness used as a proxy for plant productivity. It linked changing resource conditions with repeated glucocorticoid measurements from known elephants.

Greener landscapes accompanied lower metabolite concentrations, whereas more patchily distributed vegetation accompanied higher concentrations. Individual hormone time courses followed environmental changes even among elephants in the same family group.

Food conditions therefore influence an endocrine measure also associated with social experience. Captive assessments likewise benefit from recording seasonal resources, diet and individual sampling history. A physiological measurement becomes informative through its relationship with the biological conditions experienced before the dung sample was collected.

slides.title: Dietary restriction accompanies microbial diversity loss
body: Zhang and colleagues compared Asian elephants across completely captive, semi-captive, semi-wild and wild lifestyles. They sampled fecal bacterial communities using **16S rRNA gene sequencing**, which identifies bacterial groups from a conserved ribosomal gene.

Completely captive elephants received three principal food types, whereas wild elephants foraged approximately 112 plant species. Bacterial richness, diversity and evenness generally increased toward the wild end of the lifestyle gradient, connecting diet and living conditions with the intestinal ecosystem.

A varied foraging environment supplies different substrates to microbes as well as different sensory and motor opportunities to the elephant. Microbial **richness** concerns the number of detected groups, while **evenness** describes how balanced their abundances are. Both contribute to explaining why a restricted diet can produce a different community structure.

slides.title: Captivity changes the composition of the gut community
body: The elephant microbiome study compared bacterial composition as well as diversity. **Community composition** identifies which microbial groups are present and their relative abundances, distinguishing a change in the number of groups from a change in their identities.

The completely captive and more free-foraging lifestyles differed in families associated with the intestinal community. Ruminococcaceae showed a decreasing trend from wild to completely captive conditions, while other groups were associated with the high-fiber captive diets.

The elephant’s diet and microbial habitat form a connected biological system. Changing food variety can change the resources available to bacteria even when the total amount of food is adequate. Evaluating nutritional management therefore includes forage composition and diversity alongside body condition and observed feeding behavior.

slides.title: Microbial functional genes vary with lifestyle
body: Zhang and colleagues examined bacterial groups associated with **butyrate**, a short-chain fatty acid produced during microbial fermentation. They also measured the relative expression of a gene encoding butyryl-CoA:acetate CoA transferase, an enzyme involved in butyrate production.

The gene-expression pattern differed across lifestyles, with higher levels in semi-captive and semi-wild elephants than in completely captive and wild groups. The functional comparison therefore did not follow a simple ordering in which every measured feature increased with freedom from captivity.

Gene expression links the community record with a specific microbial process, adding information beyond taxonomy. The study’s authors proposed physiological consequences of altered fermentation. The measured elephant findings concern bacteria and functional genes; a microbiome-driven neural mechanism remains a hypothesis rather than an observed cause of stereotypy.

slides.title: Reintegration produces a changing physiological trajectory
body: Pretorius and colleagues followed African elephants through a transition from captive safari use to free living. The phases included ending rides, stabling, holding in a boma, initial release and later adaptation, allowing physiological and behavioral changes to be followed over time.

Temporal gland secretion and group-level disturbance-related behavior increased during initial release. Glucocorticoid metabolite concentrations rose later in the first year and declined by the third year toward pre-release levels. The indicators responded on different temporal scales.

Adaptation is a trajectory rather than a single moment. Measuring several phases captures initial disturbance and subsequent adjustment while preserving the delayed endocrine response. An intervention directed at welfare can therefore be evaluated through the sequence of outcomes experienced by the elephants, including the conditions supporting their longer-term transition.

slides.title: Welfare decisions depend on several lived outcomes
body: Stereotypic behavior occurred during the ridden and stable phases of the African elephant reintegration study but ceased during subsequent phases. Average glucocorticoid values before and three months after release were comparable, while temporal gland secretion increased after release.

These outcomes capture different consequences of the same transition: repetitive movement disappeared, immediate arousal-related secretion changed and the broader endocrine trajectory developed over a longer period. Combining them connects management decisions with specific behavioral and physiological experiences.

An evidence-based neuroethical assessment weighs these lived outcomes together with nutrition, health, usable environment and social opportunities. The elephant welfare assessment developed by Ghimire and colleagues combined animal-based and resource-based measures. Such an approach directs intervention toward identifiable conditions and follows whether the elephant’s opportunities and observed state improve.
